title: Sampled and graded grains and oilseeds

lessons.title: Working at a grain intake point
lessons.html:
The workplace experience

In this module you work at a real grain intake, silo, mill or grading laboratory under a mentor, sampling and grading grain and oilseeds delivered by producers or traders. You must show that you can do this correctly, safely and consistently across crops and through busy periods.

Range of work

  • Sampling trucks, bags or conveyor streams with probes and automatic samplers.
  • Reducing samples with dividers.
  • Grading a range of crops such as white and yellow maize, wheat, sunflower, soybeans and sorghum, according to the grading regulations under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990.
  • Determining moisture, screenings, foreign matter, other grain, defective kernels and crop-specific parameters.
  • Recording results and issuing grading certificates.
  • Retaining and storing reference samples.
  • Daily equipment checks.

A typical day in season

  1. Start-up: check balances with reference masses, check moisture meter, inspect sieves, confirm the system and printer work.
  2. Morning peak: sample and grade trucks in order of arrival, keeping each sample with its truck identification.
  3. Midday: check equipment again; regrade a reference sample to confirm consistency.
  4. Afternoon: continue intake; deal with any queries or disputes through the supervisor.
  5. Close-down: file certificates, store reference samples, clean the laboratory, record the day's totals.

Safety on site

  • Use sampling platforms and fall protection; never climb on loads without them.
  • Stay clear of trucks reversing or tipping.
  • Wear dust masks; grain dust irritates lungs and can be explosive in confined spaces.
  • Never enter bins, silos or pits.
  • Report any fumigation activity and keep out of fumigated areas until cleared.

Professional conduct

Producers depend on fair grading. Be courteous, explain results clearly and never let pressure, friendship or bribes influence a grade.

lessons.title: Evidence of competence
lessons.html:
What the assessor will look for

Competence means accurate results, every time, on different crops, under real conditions. Build a portfolio that shows this.

Evidence to collect

EvidenceExample
Grading recordsCopies of grading certificates you issued across several crops
Equipment check logsDaily balance and moisture meter checks you performed
Consistency checksResults of samples you graded that were regraded blind by the mentor
Observation reportsMentor checklists of you sampling and grading
Incident or dispute notesHow a disputed grade was handled
ReflectionsWhat you learned about difficult crops or defects

Accuracy targets

Agree with your mentor how your results will be compared with reference grading: for example, regraded samples should fall in the same grade and within acceptable differences on each determination. Track your own agreement over time and improve on weak areas, such as identifying specific defective kernel types.

Calculations

Show worked examples in your portfolio. For instance, a 200 g wheat sample contains 2.4 g foreign matter: 2.4 / 200 x 100 = 1.2% foreign matter. Always calculate on the correct sample mass and round as the regulations require. Example figures are illustrative.

Confidentiality

Remove producer names or contract prices from copies if the company requires, while keeping the evidence meaningful and traceable for the assessor.

Continuous improvement

Note recurring problems: queues at peak times, carry-over on sieves, moisture meter drift. Suggest improvements and record the outcome. This shows understanding beyond routine tasks.

Key points

  • Sample and grade a range of crops to current regulations.
  • Check equipment at start-up and during the day.
  • Keep samples linked to truck identity at all times.
  • Work safely: platforms, no bin entry, dust protection.
  • Collect evidence of accuracy, including blind regrading results.
